Note, Friday, Class 4. Eshaan came to me at break holding two invitations, one in each hand. One was for a classmate's cricket-match party on Saturday, and the other was for Nani's birthday lunch at the same hour. I asked only, "Which one are you thinking about?" Eshaan said, "The match has a real bat and ball and a cake." Then he went quiet. "But Nani is seventy this year and she will keep asking where I am. There will be other matches. There are not many seventieth birthdays." He put the party card in his bag and said he would tell his friend on Monday. I asked whether he was sure. He nodded. I did not say what I would choose.

Madhuri, class teacher

qa.q: How old is Nani this year?
What did Eshaan want when he said Nani would keep asking where he was?
qa.a: Eshaan wanted to be with Nani, because he cared about her and thought she would miss him more than the match would.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do to keep his friend happy?
qa.a: Eshaan could explain kindly on Monday and ask to play cricket with the friend on another day.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Eshaan arrives at the lunch?
qa.a: Nani might feel happy and loved, since Eshaan chose to be with her.

grounding: Shows a boy weighing two invitations aloud and choosing the family birthday because it matters more to him than the match.

Saturday

Two invitations for tomorrow. Binita is having everyone over to watch the big cricket final on her projector, with pizza. And it's Dadi's birthday lunch at our house, with the whole family coming. I really, really want to see the final. But I sat on the steps and thought about it. The match will be on replay, and everyone will talk about it on Monday. Dadi only turns seventy-five once. Last year she held my hand the whole time she cut her cake and said, "My boy Lokesh is here, so it's a good birthday." Family is the thing I'd feel bad about missing, not the match. So I told Binita sorry. I'll ask her who wins. I made Dadi a card with a cricket bat on it anyway 🙂

qa.q: What is Binita having everyone over for?
qa.a: To watch the big cricket final on her projector, with pizza.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel about missing the match?
qa.a: Lokesh felt torn and a bit disappointed, but decided he would feel worse about missing Dadi's birthday than the final.

qa.q: What else could Lokesh do so he doesn't miss the match completely?
qa.a: He could watch the replay later or ask Binita to call him with the score, while still being fully at Dadi's lunch.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Lokesh gives her the card?
qa.a: Dadi would likely feel touched and happy that her grandson chose to be with her 🤍

grounding: A boy invited to two events chooses his grandmother's birthday because family matters more to him than the cricket match.

passage: In the village near Kottayam, the under-12 cricket final was fixed for Sunday afternoon, the same afternoon as Ammachi's eightieth birthday. Jomon had been picked to open the batting. He sat on the rubber-tree stump behind the church for a long time. "If I play, the team has a chance. If I don't, someone else bats." He kicked a pebble. "But Ammachi Elizabeth will be eighty only once. She asked for all her grandchildren around the table." He thought of her calling him to sit beside her every evening. He walked to the coach's house before dark. "I'm sorry. My family comes first on this one." The coach nodded. On Sunday, Jomon sat next to Ammachi and cut the first slice of cake for her.

qa.a: On the rubber-tree stump behind the church.

qa.a: He felt torn and uneasy, wanting to help his team but feeling his grandmother's birthday mattered more.

qa.a: He could help practise with the new opener before Sunday, or ask a friend to call him with the score.

qa.a: The coach may be disappointed to lose an opener but probably respects that Jomon came in person to explain.
